content: This report provides detailed recommendations from the Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices (ACIP) regarding the use of specific immunizing agents for healthcare workers (HCWs) in the United States. These recommendations were developed in collaboration with the Hospital Infection Control Practices Advisory Committee (HICPAC) and align with current HICPAC guidelines for infection control among healthcare personnel. The guidance is intended to assist hospital administrators, infection control practitioners, employee health physicians, and HCWs in optimizing infection prevention and control programs. The report categorizes vaccine-preventable diseases into three groups: 1. Diseases for which active immunization is strongly recommended due to specific risks for HCWs. 2. Diseases for which immunoprophylaxis is indicated or may be indicated under certain circumstances. 3. Diseases for which protection is recommended for all adults. The recommendations reflect the most current ACIP guidance at the time of publication. For more detailed information on disease epidemiology, immunization schedules, vaccine doses, and vaccine safety and efficacy, readers are encouraged to consult individual ACIP statements and updates published in the Morbidity and Mortality Weekly Report (MMWR). Hepatitis B Hepatitis B virus (HBV) infection is a significant occupational hazard for healthcare personnel. In 1993, approximately 1,450 HCWs were infected with HBV through exposure to blood and serum-derived body fluids, representing a 90% decrease from 1985 due to vaccination and other preventive measures. Chronic HBV infection develops in 5-10% of infected individuals, potentially leading to severe complications such as chronic active hepatitis, cirrhosis, and hepatocellular carcinoma. These individuals remain infectious for life. An estimated 100-200 HCWs have died annually in the past decade due to chronic HBV-related complications. The risk of occupational HBV infection depends on the frequency of percutaneous and mucosal exposures to blood or body fluids containing blood. HCWs performing tasks involving such exposures should be vaccinated. For public safety workers with infrequent blood exposure, postexposure prophylaxis may be considered instead of routine preexposure vaccination. The Federal Standard issued under the Occupational Safety and Health Act mandates that employers provide the hepatitis B vaccine at no cost to all HCWs with occupational exposure to blood or other potentially infectious materials. Pre-vaccination serologic screening for prior infection is not required for individuals being vaccinated due to occupational risk. Booster doses are not routinely recommended, as vaccine-induced immunity has been shown to prevent clinical disease and detectable viremia even as antibody levels decline over time. Influenza Nosocomial transmission of influenza has been documented during community outbreaks, often resulting in absenteeism among medical staff and disruption of healthcare services. Influenza outbreaks in nursing homes have caused significant morbidity and mortality. Vaccination of healthcare personnel has been shown to reduce influenza-related illness and mortality among patients in long-term care facilities. Therefore, annual influenza vaccination is strongly recommended for HCWs to protect both themselves and their patients. Measles, Mumps, and Rubella Measles Nosocomial transmission of measles has been documented in various healthcare settings, including private physician offices, emergency rooms, and hospital wards. HCWs are at a significantly higher risk of measles infection compared to the general population. Vaccination is critical, as 5-9% of hospital workers born before 1957 may lack immunity to measles despite the general assumption of immunity in this age group. Mumps Outbreaks of mumps have occurred among unvaccinated adolescents and young adults, including those in healthcare settings. Primary vaccine failure has been implicated in outbreaks among highly vaccinated populations. Ensuring immunity to mumps among HCWs is prudent and can be integrated with measles and rubella control programs. Rubella Nosocomial rubella outbreaks involving both HCWs and patients have been reported. Despite widespread vaccination, 10-15% of young adults remain susceptible to rubella. Aggressive vaccination of susceptible individuals with the measles-mumps-rubella (MMR) vaccine can eliminate rubella transmission in healthcare settings. Varicella (Chickenpox) Nosocomial transmission of varicella-zoster virus (VZV) is well-documented, including airborne transmission from infected individuals to susceptible persons without direct contact. Certain patient populations, such as pregnant women, premature infants, and immunocompromised individuals, are at increased risk for severe varicella disease and complications. Strategies for controlling VZV outbreaks in hospitals include isolating infected patients, controlling airflow, and using rapid serologic testing to determine susceptibility. Vaccination is recommended for HCWs without evidence of immunity to varicella. Breakthrough infections among vaccinated individuals are generally mild, with fewer lesions and less likelihood of vesicular lesions compared to unvaccinated individuals. The risk of transmitting vaccine virus to contacts is minimal but may be higher in vaccinees who develop a varicella-like rash. Tuberculosis (TB) and Bacille Calmette-Guérin (BCG) Vaccination In the United States, BCG vaccination is not routinely recommended due to the low risk of Mycobacterium tuberculosis infection and the uncertain efficacy of the vaccine. TB prevention efforts focus on early detection and treatment of active cases, skin testing of high-risk individuals, and preventive therapy when appropriate. In certain high-risk settings, BCG vaccination may be considered as an adjunct to other control measures. Hepatitis C and Other Parenterally Transmitted Non-A, Non-B Hepatitis Hepatitis C virus (HCV) is the primary cause of parenterally transmitted non-A, non-B hepatitis in the United States. Approximately 2-4% of new HCV infections occur among HCWs exposed to blood. Chronic infection develops in 85% of cases, with 70% progressing to chronic hepatitis. Most HCV transmission is associated with percutaneous blood exposure, and HCWs are at occupational risk for acquiring this infection. Serologic enzyme immunoassays (EIAs) for detecting anti-HCV antibodies have evolved, with the latest versions detecting antibodies in ≥95% of infected individuals. However, these assays cannot distinguish between acute, chronic, or resolved infections and may yield false-positive results in low-prevalence populations. Polymerase chain reaction (PCR) testing for HCV RNA can confirm infection but is subject to variability and potential false results due to improper sample handling. Prophylaxis with immune globulins has shown limited effectiveness in preventing HCV infection. Postexposure management of HCWs should include baseline and follow-up testing for HCV markers, as well as counseling on the risk of transmission.
